```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_data <- requireNamespace("StMoMo", quietly = TRUE) && requireNamespace("demography", quietly = TRUE)
has_gg <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, eval = has_data, message = FALSE)
```

Official statistics often report deaths in 5-year age groups with an open
interval (85+ or 90+), while populations are available by single year of
age, and models are easiest to use on single years. This vignette shows how
mortensor handles such data, using Human Mortality Database (HMD) series that
are shipped with the StMoMo and demography packages:

* England & Wales, men, 1961-2011, ages 0-100 (`StMoMo::EWMaleData`);
* France, women and men, 1816-2006, ages 0-110+ (`demography::fr.mort`).

Both contain single-year deaths and exposures, so we can group them as an
official statistic would, ungroup them, and check the result against what
was actually observed.

```{r}
library(mortensor)
library(data.table)
```

## Reading HMD data

`as_mt_data()` converts the objects of both packages. Deaths and exposures
are stored per stratum (`sex`) with their age and period intervals.

```{r}
ew <- as_mt_data(StMoMo::EWMaleData)
ew
fr <- suppressWarnings(as_mt_data(demography::fr.mort, years = 1950:2006))
fr
mt_validate(fr)
```

The France data use an open 110+ interval. For HMD data downloaded directly
(an account at <https://www.mortality.org> is needed), `mt_read_hmd()` returns
the same structure:

```{r, eval = has_data && nzchar(Sys.getenv("HMD_USER"))}
swe <- mt_read_hmd("SWE", years = 1950:2020)
swe
```

## Grouping and ungrouping deaths

We group the English and Welsh deaths at ages 30-100 into 30-34, ..., 85-89
and 90-100, keep the exposures by single year, and restrict the data to
1980-2011:

```{r}
ages <- 30:100
yrs <- 1980:2011
D <- StMoMo::EWMaleData$Dxt[as.character(ages), as.character(yrs)]
E <- StMoMo::EWMaleData$Ext[as.character(ages), as.character(yrs)]
lo <- c(seq(30, 85, 5), 90)
grouped <- data.table(year = rep(yrs, each = length(lo)), age_lo = rep(lo, length(yrs)),
                      age_hi = rep(c(lo[-1], 101), length(yrs)),
                      deaths = as.vector(rowsum(D, findInterval(ages, lo))))
single <- data.table(year = rep(yrs, each = length(ages)), age_lo = rep(ages, length(yrs)),
                     age_hi = rep(ages + 1, length(yrs)), exposure = as.vector(E))
x <- mt_data(deaths = grouped, exposure = single, age = c("age_lo", "age_hi"))
x
```

`mt_ungroup()` fits the penalized composite link model (PCLM) to the deaths
of each year with the single-year exposures as offset. The latent quantity is
the rate schedule, which is smooth over age; the irregularities caused by the
size of birth cohorts stay in the exposures. Estimated deaths in each group
are scaled to the observed group total.

```{r}
t0 <- proc.time()
u1 <- mt_ungroup(x)
(proc.time() - t0)[["elapsed"]]
head(attr(u1, "ungroup"), 3)
```

```{r, eval = has_data && has_gg}
mt_plot_ungroup(x, u1, period = 2011)
```

Comparison with the observed single-year rates (median absolute log error,
which for small values is close to the relative error). The observed rates
contain Poisson noise, so even the true rates would not reach zero: the
noise floor is about 0.012 at ages 30-89 and 0.021 at 90-100.

```{r}
obs <- D / E
err <- function(u) {
  est <- mt_array(u, "deaths")[, , 1] / mt_array(u, "exposure")[, , 1]
  le <- abs(log(est / obs))
  c(ages_30_89 = median(le[ages < 90, ]), ages_90_100 = median(le[ages >= 90, ]))
}
round(err(u1), 4)
```

### Smoothing over time (2D)

With `dims = 2` the PCLM estimates a smooth age-period surface, which reduces
year-to-year noise. It is slower and, inside backtests, must be refitted on
each training window (use `step_ungroup(dims = 2)` in the preprocessing).

```{r}
x_recent <- mt_subset(x, periods = c(2000, NA))
u2 <- mt_ungroup(x_recent, dims = 2)
attr(u2, "ungroup")
obs_recent <- obs[, as.character(2000:2011)]
est2 <- mt_array(u2, "deaths")[, , 1] / mt_array(u2, "exposure")[, , 1]
est1 <- (mt_array(u1, "deaths")[, , 1] / mt_array(u1, "exposure")[, , 1])[, as.character(2000:2011)]
mae <- function(est) {
  le <- abs(log(est / obs_recent))
  c(ages_30_89 = median(le[ages < 90, ]), ages_90_100 = median(le[ages >= 90, ]))
}
round(rbind(dims_1 = mae(est1), dims_2 = mae(est2)), 4)
```

```{r, eval = has_data && has_gg, fig.height = 3.5}
long <- rbind(
  data.table(source = "observed", year = 2000:2011, rate = obs_recent["95", ]),
  data.table(source = "PCLM 1D", year = 2000:2011, rate = est1["95", ]),
  data.table(source = "PCLM 2D", year = 2000:2011, rate = est2["95", ]))
ggplot2::ggplot(long, ggplot2::aes(year, rate, colour = source)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line() + ggplot2::geom_point(size = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "Death rate at age 95", colour = NULL) +
  scale_colour_mortensor(type = "categorical") +
  theme_mortensor()
```

### Without exposures

If only deaths are available, they can be ungrouped as counts per year of
age. mortensor warns, because the split of the oldest group (here 90-100)
is then determined by the smoothness assumption alone, and refuses 2D
smoothing of counts: cohort-size waves run diagonally through the
age-period surface of death counts and cannot be represented by a smooth
surface.

```{r}
x_counts <- x
x_counts$obs$exposure <- NULL
uc <- mt_ungroup(x_counts)
est_c <- mt_array(uc, "deaths")[, , 1] / E
round(c(ages_30_89 = median(abs(log(est_c / obs))[ages < 90, ]),
        ages_90_100 = median(abs(log(est_c / obs))[ages >= 90, ])), 3)
```

```{r, error = TRUE}
mt_ungroup(x_counts, dims = 2)
```

## Grouped exposures and open intervals

For France we group the exposures at ages 30-84 into 5-year groups, keep the
open interval 85+, and ungroup them again. Exposures are counts, so they are
ungrouped without offset; the monotone spline of cumulative exposures
reproduces group totals exactly.

```{r}
fr2 <- mt_regroup(mt_subset(fr, periods = c(1990, NA)), age = 30:85)
fr_grouped <- fr2
fr_grouped$obs$exposure <- mt_regroup(fr2, age = seq(30, 85, 5))$obs$exposure
fr_grouped$obs$deaths <- NULL
fr_grouped <- mt_set_grid(fr_grouped, age = single_ages(30, 85))
truth <- mt_array(fr2, "exposure")
for (method in c("pclm", "monotone")) {
  est <- mt_array(mt_ungroup(fr_grouped, exposure_method = method), "exposure")
  cat(sprintf("%-9s median abs log error, ages 30-84: %.4f\n", method, median(abs(log(est / truth))[1:55, , ])))
}
```

Splitting the **open** interval itself is a different matter. Asking for
single years up to 100+ forces the method to extrapolate the age pattern
inside 85+ from the totals alone; mortensor warns, and the comparison with
the observed exposures shows why:

```{r}
fr3 <- mt_regroup(mt_subset(fr, periods = c(1990, NA)), age = 30:100)
fr3_grouped <- fr3
fr3_grouped$obs$exposure <- mt_regroup(fr3, age = seq(30, 85, 5))$obs$exposure
fr3_grouped$obs$deaths <- NULL
fr3_grouped <- mt_set_grid(fr3_grouped, age = single_ages(30, 100))
est <- mt_array(mt_ungroup(fr3_grouped), "exposure")
le <- abs(log(est / mt_array(fr3, "exposure")))
round(c(ages_85_99 = median(le[56:70, , ]), age_100_plus = median(le[71, , ])), 2)
```

Errors of this size (a factor of several at 100+) make such estimates
unusable. Use population data with a higher open age (single-year
populations up to 100+ are published by many statistical offices), or keep
the open interval of the grid where the data have it.

## Regrouping

`mt_regroup()` aggregates exactly. Cells that would straddle a target
boundary raise an error; target cells that are only partly observed are
dropped with a warning.

```{r}
mt_regroup(fr, age = c(0, 1, seq(5, 100, 5)), period = seq(1950, 2005, 5))
```

## Summary

* Ungroup deaths as rates, with exposures on the target grid as offset.
  On these HMD data the error is close to the Poisson noise of the observed
  single-year rates.
* Ungroup exposures first when only grouped exposures are available, but do
  not split an open interval of exposures from its total alone.
* Deaths without exposures can be ungrouped in 1D, with weak information
  about the oldest ages.
* Inside forecasting pipelines, ungrouping is a preprocessing step that is
  refitted on each training window (see the forecasting vignette).
